Use HIFLD Next's hospital layer (version 1.1.0, find it with the MCP tools) and Heimdall Research's Storm Blackout and Restoration tables, version 1.2, on Zenodo: record 23010005, files listed at https://zenodo.org/api/records/23010005 (a file named X downloads from https://zenodo.org/api/records/23010005/files/X/content; the data dictionary is docs__DATA_DICTIONARY.md). Count a storm against a county when at least 10% of the county's customers were out at the peak and it took more than 72 hours to get 90% of them back, including counties never restored within the data's window. Use only FEMA-declared counties with utility records. Keep open hospitals only. Report how many hospitals, hospital-storm pairs and storms qualify, how many hospitals qualify in more than one storm, the 10 hospitals with the most qualifying storms, and a count by trauma level.

# Data dictionary: Storm Blackout and Restoration, version 1.2

One entry per column of every table: its type, unit, meaning, and when it is empty and why. An empty cell means the value was not measured. It is never written as 0. Read the code columns (`geoid`, `region_id`, `area_id`, `context_for_region_id`, `county_geoid`, `state_fips`) as text to keep their leading zeros.

County rows for tribal-area storms are context: they describe the whole county, not the tribal area, and tribal nations are sovereign areas. The share fields say how much of each county lies inside the area.

Radiance from different products should not be compared between storms; this release gives no conversion between them. `product` says which one a storm uses.

## `storms.csv`

One row per storm, including the storms that have no night-light numbers or no outage run. Key: `event_id`.

| Column | Type | Unit | Meaning | When empty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `event_id` | string |  | NHC storm identifier (for example AL092022) or FEMA disaster number (DR-4901) | Never empty |
| `name` | string |  | Storm name or FEMA declaration title | Never empty |
| `kind` | string |  | Storm type from the NHC record or the FEMA incident type. Values: `tropical`, `typhoon`, `winter_storm`, `severe_ice_storm`, `snowstorm`, `severe_storm`, `coastal_storm`, `straight-line_winds`, `tornado`, `flood` | Never empty |
| `landfall` | date |  | UTC date of the first HURDAT2 landfall on a U.S. state (the first on a territory when there was none on a state). For FEMA-numbered storms, the FEMA incident begin date | Never empty |
| `landfall_time_utc` | string |  | UTC time of that landfall, HH:MM | No landfall time in the source: FEMA-numbered storms, and tropical storms whose date comes from the catalog without a HURDAT2 landfall record |
| `first_impact_date` | date |  | UTC date the storm centre first came within 250 km of a county in the table, when that is two or more days before landfall. The baseline nights end before it | The storm reached no county two or more days before landfall |
| `states` | string |  | Declared states and territories, space separated | Never empty |
| `source` | string |  | Where the landfall date and time come from | Never empty |
| `night_light_unit` | string |  | county: night light by county. tribal_area: night light by tribal area, for a tribal declaration with no county named. Values: `county`, `tribal_area` | The storm has no night-light numbers. night_light_reason says why |
| `night_light_reason` | string |  | Why the storm has no night-light numbers. before_nasa_record: the storm window starts before the VNP46A2 record begins on 2012-01-19. territory_not_in_county_boundaries: Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands or American Samoa, which the county boundary file does not cover. Values: `before_nasa_record`, `territory_not_in_county_boundaries` | The storm has night-light numbers |
| `product` | string |  | Night-light product the storm is measured with: VNP46A2 (Suomi NPP) or VJ146A2 (NOAA-20). One product per storm. Radiance from different products should not be compared between storms. Values: `VNP46A2`, `VJ146A2` | The storm has no night-light numbers. night_light_reason says why |
| `outage_reason` | string |  | Why the storm has no county outage run. no_utility_record_before_2014: before the public EAGLE-I county series starts on 2014-11-01. no_published_year: no EAGLE-I file is published for the year. no_county_outage_record: a tribal declaration that names no county. territory_not_in_eaglei: a territory EAGLE-I does not cover. Values: `no_utility_record_before_2014`, `no_published_year`, `no_county_outage_record`, `territory_not_in_eaglei` | The storm has an outage run. Its rows are in utility_by_county |
| `window_note` | string |  | window_cut_at_source_end: the 45-day outage window runs past 31 December 2025, the last day of the published EAGLE-I record, so records stop there. Values: `window_cut_at_source_end` | The outage window is not cut, or the storm has no outage run |
| `also_known_as` | string |  | FEMA disaster numbers for the same storm that have no row of their own, space separated (for example DR-4466 on Imelda, AL112019). Each such declaration names the same counties on the same date, and its outage records are the same | No other number is recorded for the storm |

## `county_summary.csv`

One row per storm and county with night light (method v3), with the outage columns joined from utility_by_county. Key: `event_id`, `geoid`.
Every row joins `storms` on `event_id`, and holds the same `product`.
One product per storm: `product` is one value within each `event_id`.
A wind radius is on file for a storm or it is not: `in_nhc_wind_radius` is empty in every row or in none within each `event_id`.

| Column | Type | Unit | Meaning | When empty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `event_id` | string |  | NHC storm identifier (for example AL092022) or FEMA disaster number (DR-4901) | Never empty |
| `geoid` | string |  | County FIPS code, 5 digits. Read as text to keep the leading zero | Never empty |
| `county` | string |  | County name | Never empty |
| `state` | string |  | State or territory postal code | Never empty |
| `declared` | boolean |  | True when FEMA declared the county for this storm | Never empty |
| `declared_via` | string |  | The declaration that names the county: major_disaster, or emergency for a tropical storm's emergency declaration. A county named in both is major_disaster. Values: `major_disaster`, `emergency` | The county is not declared for this storm |
| `in_nhc_wind_radius` | boolean |  | True when the county lies inside the NHC 34-knot wind radius of the storm, False when it lies outside | No wind radius is on file for the storm (filled for the 34 Atlantic storms HURDAT2 gives a radius for). Empty does not mean outside |
| `product` | string |  | Night-light product the storm is measured with: VNP46A2 (Suomi NPP) or VJ146A2 (NOAA-20). One product per storm. Radiance from different products should not be compared between storms. Values: `VNP46A2`, `VJ146A2` | Never empty |
| `baseline_radiance` | number | nW/cm²/sr | Median radiance of the clear baseline nights before the storm | baseline_source is insufficient: there were no baseline nights |
| `baseline_nights` | integer |  | Clear nights in the baseline | Never empty |
| `baseline_source` | string |  | event_window: baseline nights before the storm. prior_year: the same season a year earlier, used when the nights before the storm were too few. insufficient: no baseline. Values: `event_window`, `prior_year`, `insufficient` | Never empty |
| `post_obs_nights` | integer |  | Nights with usable pixels after the landfall date | Never empty |
| `median_valid_pixel_share` | number |  | Median share of usable pixels after the landfall date | Never empty |
| `status` | string |  | What the night-light series did. It is not a detected power outage. light_drop: smoothed light fell below the county's normal range soon after impact. no_measurable_outage: observed, no such fall (the name keeps an old use of the word outage for a night-light state). cloud_obscured: not observed until late and normal by then. low_signal: too noisy to judge. insufficient_data: too few nights. Values: `light_drop`, `no_measurable_outage`, `cloud_obscured`, `low_signal`, `insufficient_data` | Never empty |
| `outage_min_ratio` | number |  | Lowest smoothed light ratio after impact (a night-light value despite the name) | status is low_signal or insufficient_data |
| `outage_min_day` | integer | days | Day of that lowest ratio, counted from impact_date | status is low_signal or insufficient_data |
| `days_to_50` | integer | days | Days from impact until smoothed light was back at or above 50% of baseline | Not measured. days_to_50_reason says why |
| `days_to_50_reason` | string |  | Why days_to_50 is empty. never_below_50: a light_drop status, but light never fell below 50%. not_back_to_50_in_window: fell below 50% and did not return. no_outage_measured: observed, no light drop found (a night-light state despite the name). not_observed_cloud, not_observed_too_few_nights: the county was not observed. not_measurable_low_signal: its light is too noisy to judge. Values: `never_below_50`, `not_back_to_50_in_window`, `no_outage_measured`, `not_observed_cloud`, `not_observed_too_few_nights`, `not_measurable_low_signal` | days_to_50 has a value |
| `days_to_normal` | integer | days | Days from impact until smoothed light was back in the county's normal range | Not measured. days_to_normal_reason says why |
| `days_to_normal_reason` | string |  | Why days_to_normal is empty. not_back_to_normal_in_window: a light_drop status that did not return to normal. The other codes are as in days_to_50_reason. Values: `not_back_to_normal_in_window`, `no_outage_measured`, `not_observed_cloud`, `not_observed_too_few_nights`, `not_measurable_low_signal` | days_to_normal has a value |
| `recovery_uncertain` | boolean |  | True when a gap of 5 or more days without a clear night comes just before days_to_normal | days_to_normal is empty |
| `window_end_day` | integer | days | Last day of the night-light window, counted from impact_date | Never empty |
| `window_end_reason` | string |  | window: the full window. data_end: the stored nights stop earlier. next_storm:DR-number: the next FEMA storm in the county | Never empty |
| `impact_date` | date |  | Date the storm reached the county, day 0 of the window | Never empty |
| `impact_source` | string |  | How impact_date was chosen. track_within_250km: first UTC date the HURDAT2 track came within 250 km of the county. track_closest_approach: the track never came that close, so the date of closest approach. catalog_landfall: storms.landfall. Values: `track_within_250km`, `track_closest_approach`, `catalog_landfall` | Never empty |
| `clear_nights_pre` | integer |  | Clear nights before impact | Never empty |
| `clear_nights_post` | integer |  | Clear nights after impact | Never empty |
| `method_version` | string |  | Night-light method version. Values: `v3` | Never empty |
| `source_night_light` | string |  | Layer marker. Values: `night_light` | Never empty |
| `post_days_window` | integer | days | Days after the landfall date covered by stored nights | Never empty |
| `available` | boolean |  | True when utility records cover this county's window | Never empty |
| `reason` | string |  | Utility availability. ok: records in the window. no_rows_in_window: rows that year but none in the window. no_utility_record: no EAGLE-I rows for the county that year. county_not_declared: the outage run reads declared counties only. no_utility_record_before_2014, no_published_year: the storm-level outage_reason, for a storm with no outage run. Values: `ok`, `no_rows_in_window`, `no_utility_record`, `county_not_declared`, `no_utility_record_before_2014`, `no_published_year` | Never empty |
| `source` | string |  | utility_records when the county has EAGLE-I rows in the window, otherwise none. Values: `utility_records`, `none` | Never empty |
| `peak_customers_out` | number |  | Peak customers out reported in EAGLE-I, taken after readings that hold more than one collection snapshot are replaced (see flagged_readings). A replaced reading is an interpolated value that was not measured | No utility record for the county in the window. peak_reason is set and reason says why |
| `peak_reason` | string |  | Why peak_customers_out is empty: no_utility_record. reason gives the cause (for example county_not_declared). Values: `no_utility_record` | peak_customers_out has a value |
| `peak_customers_out_raw` | number |  | Highest reading in the window as the EAGLE-I year file records it, before any filter | peak_customers_out is empty |
| `flagged_readings` | integer |  | Readings in the window that held more than one collection snapshot and were replaced. 0 when none | peak_customers_out is empty |
| `peak_share_out` | number |  | peak_customers_out divided by customers_total | No share. peak_share_reason says why |
| `peak_share_reason` | string |  | Why peak_share_out is empty. no_utility_record: no EAGLE-I rows. no_customers_total: customers_total is empty and customers_reason says why. peak_above_customer_estimate: the peak is above the customer estimate. Values: `no_customers_total`, `no_utility_record`, `peak_above_customer_estimate` | peak_share_out has a value |

| `hours_to_90pct_reason` | string |  | Why hours_to_90pct_restored is empty. not_restored_in_window: still above 10% of the peak at the end. no_customers_out: the peak is 0. no_utility_record: no EAGLE-I rows. reporting_drop: a one-step collapse of the feed is what crossed the threshold. peak_mismatch: the 15-minute series does not reproduce the published peak. Values: `not_restored_in_window`, `no_customers_out`, `no_utility_record`, `reporting_drop`, `peak_mismatch` | hours_to_90pct_restored has a value |

items.description: This feature class/shapefile contains locations of Hospitals for 50 US states, Washington D.C., US territories of Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa, Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, and Virgin Islands. The dataset only includes hospital facilities based on data acquired from various state departments or federal sources which has been referenced in the SOURCE field. Hospital facilities which do not occur in these sources will be not present in the database. The source data was available in a variety of formats (pdfs, tables, webpages, etc.) which was cleaned and geocoded and then converted into a spatial database. The database does not contain nursing homes or health centers. Hospitals have been categorized into children, chronic disease, critical access, general acute care, long term care, military, psychiatric, rehabilitation, special, and women based on the range of the available values from the various sources after removing similarities.

items.name: Broadband Radio Service (BRS) and Educational Broadband Service (EBS) Transmitters
items.description: The Broadband Radio Service (BRS), formerly known as the Multipoint Distribution Service (MDS)/Multichannel Multipoint Distribution Service (MMDS), is a commercial service. In the past, it was generally used for the transmission of data and video programming to subscribers using high-powered systems, also known as wireless cable. However, over the years, the uses have evolved to include digital two-way systems capable of providing high-speed, high-capacity broadband service, including two-way Internet service via cellularized communication systems. Such services provide consumers integrated access to voice, high-speed data, video-on-demand, and interactive delivery services from a wireless device. The Educational Broadband Service (EBS), formerly known as the Instructional Television Fixed Service (ITFS), is an educational service that has generally been used for the transmission of instructional material to accredited educational institutions and non-educational institutions such as hospitals, nursing homes, training centers, and rehabilitation centers using high-powered systems. Our recent revamping of the EBS spectrum will now make it possible for EBS users to continue their instructional services utilizing low-power broadband systems while also providing students with high-speed internet access.The 2.5 GHz band, which is divided into the Broadband Radio Service (BRS) and the Educational Broadband Service (EBS), is available for commercial service. The band is currently used to provide high-speed, high-capacity broadband service, including two-way Internet service via cellularized communication systems. Such services provide consumers integrated access to voice, high-speed data, video-on-demand, and interactive delivery services from a wireless device. items.name: Veterans Health Administration Medical Facilities
items.description: The Veterans Health Administration Medical Facilities dataset includes Veteran Affairs hospitals, Veteran Affairs Residential Rehabilitation Treatment Programs (RRTP), Veteran Affairs Nursing Home Care Units (NHCU), Veteran Affairs Outpatient Clinics (VAOC), Vet Centers, and Veteran Affairs Medical Centers (VAMC). It should not include planned and suspended (non-operational) sites and mobile clinics. These definitions were set by the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) Policy Board in December 1998 and are the basis for defining the category and the additional service types for each VHA service site. These definitions cover sites generally owned by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) with the exception of leased and contracted community-based outpatient clinics (CBOCs). 1. VA HOSPITAL: an institution (health care site) that is owned, staffed and operated by VA and whose primary function is to provide inpatient services. NOTE: Each geographically unique inpatient division of an integrated facility is counted as a separate hospital. 2. VA RESIDENTIAL REHABILITATION TREATMENT PROGRAM (RRTP): provides comprehensive health and social services in a VA facility for eligible veterans who are ambulatory and do not require the level of care provided in nursing homes. 3. VA NURSING HOME CARE UNITS (NHCU): provides care to individuals who are not in need of hospital care, but who require nursing care and related medical or psychosocial services in an institutional setting. VA NHCUs are facilities designed to care for patients who require a comprehensive care management system coordinated by an interdisciplinary team. Services provided include nursing, medical, rehabilitative, recreational, dietetic, psychosocial, pharmaceutical, radiological, laboratory, dental and spiritual. 4. VA OUTPATIENT CLINICS: a. Community-Based Outpatient Clinic (CBOC): a VA-operated, VA-funded, or VA-reimbursed health care facility or site geographically distinct or separate from a parent medical facility. This term encompasses all types of VA outpatient clinics, except hospital-based, independent and mobile clinics. Satellite, community-based, and outreach clinics have been redefined as CBOCs. Technically, CBOCs fall into four Categories, which are: > (i) VA-owned. A CBOC that is owned and staffed by VA. > (ii) Leased. A CBOC where the space is leased (contracted), but is staffed by VA. NOTE: This includes donated space staffed by VA. > (iii) Contracted. A CBOC where the space and the staff are not VA. This is typically a Healthcare Management Organization (HMO)-type provided where multiple sites can be associated with a single station identifier. > (iv) Not Operational. A CBOC which has been approved by Congress, but has not yet begun operating. b. Hospital-Based Outpatient Clinic: outpatient clinic functions located at a hospital. c. Independent Outpatient Clinic: a full-time, self-contained, freestanding, ambulatory care clinic that has no management, program, or fiscal relationship to a VA medical facility. Primary and specialty health care services are provided in an outpatient setting. 5. VET CENTER: Provides professional readjustment counseling, community education, outreach to special populations, brokering of services with community agencies, and access to links between the veteran and VA. 6. VA MEDICAL CENTER (VAMC): a medical center is a unique VA site of care providing two or more types of services that reside at a single physical site location. The services provided are the primary service as tracked in the VHA Site Tracking (VAST) (i.e., VA Hospital, Nursing Home, Domiciliary, independent outpatient clinic (IOC), hospital-based outpatient clinic (HBOC), and CBOC). The definition of VA medical center does not include the Vet Centers as an identifying service. This dataset is based upon GFI data received from the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). At the request of NGA, text fields in this dataset have been set to all upper case to facilitate consistent database engine search results. At the request of NGA, all diacritics (e.g., the German umlaut or the Spanish tilde) have been replaced with their closest equivalent English character to facilitate use with database systems that may not support diacritics. The currentness of this dataset is indicated by the [CONTDATE] attribute. Based upon this attribute, the oldest record dates from 09/21/2007 and the newest record dates from 10/15/2007.

# Storm Blackout and Restoration

Not for real-time emergency response or for any decision about one address or property.

Not in this download, free through the API: lights-out videos for most storms, storm-path videos for hurricanes and tropical storms, forecast maps and satellite loops. Get a free key at https://heimdallresearch.com/go/signup

Night light data: NASA Black Marble (VNP46A2, VJ146A2), courtesy of NASA LAADS DAAC. Roman et al. (2018), DOI 10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017.

Utility outage data: EAGLE-I / ORNL, Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.24237376 (CC BY 4.0).

Customer estimates: U.S. Energy Information Administration Form EIA-861 and U.S. Census Bureau county housing unit estimates (public domain).

Declarations, boundaries and tracks: OpenFEMA, U.S. Census Bureau cartographic boundary files and NOAA NHC best tracks (public domain).

Not for real-time emergency response or for any decision about one address or property. Provided as is, without warranty of any kind.

County records for 672 FEMA-declared U.S. storms with landfall or incident dates from 2012-01-14 to 2026-08-11: NASA Black Marble night light by county and night, and reported power outages and restoration times from DOE EAGLE-I utility records where they exist.

The catalog lists 672 storms in `storms.csv`. 658 have night-light numbers:
611 by county and 47 by tribal area. 477 have
an outage run on EAGLE-I, and 464 of these have records for at least one county.
Every storm without numbers keeps its row, with a reason code in `night_light_reason` or `outage_reason`.

Night light is the county mean of NASA Black Marble daily radiance over valid pixels, one night per row in
`county_daily.csv`, with a per-county summary in `county_summary.csv`. Each storm is measured with one product,
named in `product`. Radiance from different products should not be compared between storms; this release gives no
conversion between them.

The outage columns come from EAGLE-I county customers out (Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.24237376) for the
declared counties of each storm, in a 45-day window from each county's impact date.

47 storms were declared for a tribal area with no county named. They ship as tribal-area
rows (`tribal_area_summary.csv`, `tribal_area_daily.csv`) and county context rows (`region_role` is
`county_context`). County rows for tribal-area storms are context: they describe the whole county, not the tribal
area, and tribal nations are sovereign areas. The share fields say how much of each county lies inside the area.

An empty cell means the value was not measured. It is never written as 0. A column that can be empty for more
than one reason has a reason column beside it, and `docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.md` says for every column when it is
empty and why.

## Key figures

- Storms in the catalog: 672
- Storms with night-light numbers: 658
- Storms with an outage run: 477
- Counties and county equivalents with night light: 3,194
- Storm-county rows with utility records in the window: 10,260
- Median peak customers out over storm-county rows with reason ok: 1,766
- Median hours to 90% restored, storm-county rows where it was measured: 30.2 hours

## What the data shows

### Irma has the largest sum of county outage peaks among these 672 storm events: 8.9 million.

Among these 672 storm events, Irma (AL112017) has the largest sum of county peak customers out: **8,867,374** across **329** counties with a numeric peak. Each county contributes its own peak. Those peaks are not one simultaneous count of customers out.

If you are comparing these storm events, this shows the scale of Irma's county peaks. It is not an outage feed for one day and not a figure for one address.

```python
import pandas as pd
u = pd.read_csv("data/utility_by_county.csv")
x = u.assign(p=pd.to_numeric(u.peak_customers_out, errors="coerce")).dropna(subset=["p"])
g = x.groupby("event_id").p.agg(["sum","count"]).sort_values("sum", ascending=False)
print(len(pd.read_csv("data/storms.csv")), g.index[0], int(g.iloc[0]["sum"]), int(g.iloc[0]["count"]))
```

### Milton's sum of county outage peaks ranks fifth: 3.7 million.

Milton (AL142024) sums to **3,736,269** peak customers across **51** counties (**5th** largest sum). Each county contributes its own peak.

Milton is a Florida landfall in this package. Compare its summed peaks with the other storm events in this table.

```python
import pandas as pd
u = pd.read_csv("data/utility_by_county.csv")
x = u.assign(p=pd.to_numeric(u.peak_customers_out, errors="coerce")).dropna(subset=["p"])
g = x.groupby("event_id").p.agg(["sum","count"]).sort_values("sum", ascending=False)
print(int(g.loc["AL142024","sum"]), int(g.loc["AL142024","count"]), list(g.index).index("AL142024")+1)
```

### After Maria, night-light brightness took 121 days to return to the usual range in the typical county.

For Maria (AL152017), the median of days_to_normal is **121** days across **46** counties with a value. This column is satellite night-light brightness.

Grid restoration hours and satellite night-light recovery answer different questions on the same storm. Maria's night-light timing sits in Puerto Rico and USVI context in this package.

```python
import pandas as pd
c = pd.read_csv("data/county_summary.csv")
d = pd.to_numeric(c[c.event_id=="AL152017"].days_to_normal, errors="coerce").dropna()
print(int(d.median()), int(d.size))
```

### After Irma, the typical county reached 90% of customers restored in 53 hours.

For Irma, the median county hours to 90 percent restored is **52.9** hours (**280** counties with a numeric value).

If you need both clocks on Irma, read this next to the Maria night-light finding. Utility restoration timing and night-light timing are not the same measure.

```python
import pandas as pd
u = pd.read_csv("data/utility_by_county.csv")
h = pd.to_numeric(u[u.event_id=="AL112017"].hours_to_90pct_restored, errors="coerce").dropna()
print(round(float(h.median()),1), int(h.size))
```

### 44 of 672 storm events are tropical cyclones or typhoons.

These **672** storm events include **36** with kind tropical and **8** with kind typhoon (**44** together). Kind tropical includes hurricanes. Other counts: severe storms **347**, floods **186**, tornadoes **24**, ice storms **21**, winter storms **21**, snowstorms **20**, straight-line wind **6**, coastal storms **3**.

If you expected only hurricanes, check this first. Severe storms and floods are the two largest counts. Kind tropical includes hurricanes.

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.read_csv("data/storms.csv")
u = pd.read_csv("data/utility_by_county.csv")
x = u.assign(p=pd.to_numeric(u.peak_customers_out, errors="coerce")).dropna(subset=["p"])
print(len(s), s.kind.isin(["tropical", "typhoon"]).sum(), s.kind.value_counts().to_dict(), list(x.groupby("event_id").p.sum().nlargest(3).index))
```

## Coverage

| | |
|---|---|
| Publisher | Heimdall Research |
| Version | 1.2 |
| Released | 2026-10-10 |
| Version DOI | [10.5281/zenodo.23010005](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23010005) |
| Concept DOI | 10.5281/zenodo.23010004 (all versions) |
| License | CC BY 4.0 |
| Web page | https://heimdallresearch.com/data/storm-blackout/ |
| Period | 2012-01-14 to 2026-08-11 (672 storms) |
| Resolution | County by day, and tribal area by day for tribal declarations |
| Update cadence | This catalog runs through 2026-08-11. New storms are not added on a schedule. |

## Versions

| Version | Where published |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | Kaggle |
| 1.1 | Kaggle |
| 1.2 | Zenodo, Kaggle, Hugging Face (first version on Zenodo and Hugging Face) |

Versions 1.0 and 1.1 were published on Kaggle only and have no Zenodo DOI. Version 1.2 is the first version on Zenodo and Hugging Face.

Spatial units:

| area | period | storms | counties | tribal_areas |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States, Puerto Rico and U.S. Virgin Islands, with Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa as storm rows only | 2012-01-14 to 2026-08-11 | 672 | 3,194 | 28 |

## Research use

Questions the tables can answer, each with the table and columns it uses, and what the tables leave open: [docs/RESEARCH_USE.md](docs/RESEARCH_USE.md).

## Method

- Storms: `storms.csv` lists FEMA-declared hurricanes, tropical storms, typhoons, winter storms, severe storms and floods. `storms.landfall` is the UTC date of the first HURDAT2 landfall on a U.S. state (the first on a territory when there was none on a state). For FEMA-numbered storms it is the incident begin date. `storms.source` gives the source of each date. A FEMA disaster that is the same storm as an NHC storm, with the same landfall date, states, declared counties and outage records, has no row of its own: its number is in `also_known_as` of the NHC storm. The NHC storm's night-light rows are kept, because their impact dates come from the track.
- Declared counties: a county is declared when the storm's major disaster declaration names it. For tropical storms it is also declared when the storm's emergency declaration names it, matched by year and storm name in the declaration title. A title that names two storms counts for both. `declared_via` says which. A county named in both is `major_disaster`.
- Night light: NASA Black Marble daily radiance (VNP46A2 on Suomi NPP, VJ146A2 on NOAA-20), dataset DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL. The gap-filled dataset is not read. A pixel is valid when it has a value, Mandatory_Quality_Flag is 0, the cloud mask says confident clear and Snow_Flag is 0. County radiance for a night is the sum of radiance over the county's valid pixels, from every tile it touches, divided by the number of those pixels. It is empty when there is no valid pixel.
- One product per storm: the baseline and the nights after the storm come from the same satellite, and `product` names it.
- Boundaries: Census cartographic boundary file cb_2024_us_county_500k for counties, cb_2020_us_county_500k for the eight Connecticut counties, and cb_2024_us_aiannh_500k for tribal areas. The file hashes are in `census_boundaries_manifest.json`.
- Summary: each county has an impact date from the HURDAT2 track (first date within 250 km, or the date of closest approach), or the catalog landfall date. Clear nights are smoothed with a 5-night rolling median and compared with the county's own range before the storm, giving `status`, `days_to_50` and `days_to_normal`.
- Outage: EAGLE-I county customers out for the declared counties of each storm, in a 45-day window from each county's impact date. The window ends earlier at the next FEMA storm in the county (`outage_window_end_reason`). Readings that hold more than one collection snapshot are flagged and replaced before peaks, customer-hours and restore hours are taken. Restore times count hours from the peak until customers out stay at or below 50% and 10% of the peak for 6 hours. Outage method v2. A reporting drop is one 15-minute step that cuts the outage by more than 25% of the county peak and lands at or below 10% of the previous reading. When that low spell lasts the 6-hour sustain and the feed does not return to at least half the pre-drop reading within 12 hours, the restore hours that the spell would have set are empty with reason `reporting_drop`, and `reporting_drop` is true. Customer-hours stop at that step (`customer_hours_reason`). If the feed returns within 12 hours, those readings are skipped and the hours are read from the series after the return. No restoration time is filled in. A reading at the start or end of a county series has only the reading beside it. The spike rule looks at both sides, so it leaves that reading in place. When setting it to the reading beside it makes the recomputed peak match the published peak, the restore hours are read from that series. Where the 15-minute series does not reproduce the published peak, the restore hours are empty with reason `peak_mismatch` and the peak is left as published.

**Intended use:** Comparing reported outages and restoration times across counties and storms, and studying how county night light changes after a storm.

**Not intended for:** Real-time emergency response, any decision about a single address or property, or statements about a tribal area drawn from county rows.

## Limits and appropriate use

- Night light is related to electricity service but is a different quantity. Generators can restore light before the grid does, and damaged or empty buildings can stay dark after power returns. `status`, `days_to_50` and `days_to_normal` come from night light alone. Scored against reported outages, the result is weak. County mean darkness (dark_county_mean) does not separate counties with large outages from counties with small ones: pooled AUC 0.515 over 418 storms and 5,841 counties, 95% interval 0.482 to 0.547 from resampling storms. The interval includes 0.5, which is chance. Lit-pixel radiance drop (dark_lit_ratio) separates counties with large outages from counties with small ones: pooled AUC 0.559 over 287 storms and 3,611 counties, 95% interval 0.511 to 0.605 from resampling storms. Change in the share of unlit lit-mask pixels (dark_lit_share) separates counties with large outages from counties with small ones: pooled AUC 0.566 over 287 storms and 3,611 counties, 95% interval 0.513 to 0.615 from resampling storms. An AUC of 0.5 is a coin flip. Use the utility columns for outage size and restoration time.
- Radiance from different products should not be compared between storms; this release gives no conversion between them. 500 storms use VNP46A2 and 158 use VJ146A2 (`product`). Compare radiance within a storm, or between storms on the same product.
- County rows for tribal-area storms are context: they describe the whole county, not the tribal area, and tribal nations are sovereign areas. The share fields say how much of each county lies inside the area. The 47 tribal declarations have no county list, so they have tribal-area rows and overlapping-county context rows only and are absent from `county_summary.csv` and `county_daily.csv`. Their outage and customer columns are empty: EAGLE-I reports counties (`no_county_outage_record`) and EIA-861 customer counts are by county (`no_county_customer_count`). Outage records for the overlapping counties of 41 of these storms are in `tribal_context_utility_by_county.csv`, as context.
- Henri (AL082021) lists MA in `states` because of FEMA EM-3566-MA, an emergency declaration for the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe that names no county. Its 14 Massachusetts rows in `county_summary.csv` are measured but not declared (`reason` is `county_not_declared`), and the tribal area, which lies in Barnstable and Bristol counties, is not measured for this storm.
- `thin_region` is True for a tribal area with fewer than 20 pixels on its tiles. `thin_night` is True for a county or area night with 1 to 19 valid pixels. Both keep the value as measured, and such values are noisy.
- 14 storms have no night-light numbers: 3 have a storm window that starts before the VNP46A2 record begins on 2012-01-19 (`before_nasa_record`), and 11 are in Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands or American Samoa, which the county boundary file does not cover (`territory_not_in_county_boundaries`).
- 195 storms have no outage run: 117 predate the public EAGLE-I county series, which starts 2014-11-01 (`no_utility_record_before_2014`). 30 fall in a year with no published EAGLE-I file (`no_published_year`). 41 are tribal declarations with no county named (`no_county_outage_record`). 7 are in territories EAGLE-I does not cover (`territory_not_in_eaglei`).
- 13 storms have an outage run but no county with EAGLE-I records in the window, so none of their `utility_by_county.csv` rows has `reason` `ok`: AL152017, DR-4227, DR-4271, DR-4275, DR-4296, DR-4306, DR-4311, DR-4327, DR-4388, DR-4571, DR-4609, DR-4649, DR-4805. Their rows give `no_utility_record` or `no_rows_in_window`, and their outage columns are empty.
- The 6 late-2025 storms (DR-4901, DR-4902, DR-4903, DR-4905, DR-4906, DR-4907) have an outage window that ends 31 December 2025, the last day of the published EAGLE-I record (`window_note` is `window_cut_at_source_end`). `outage_window_end_day` gives the planned window for these storms, and their records stop earlier.
- Customer-hours for counties in both version 1.1 and this table: Matthew (AL142016) sums to 140,943,783.1 in version 1.1 and 140,435,077.7 here (70 of 181 counties differ); Irma (AL112017) sums to 595,686,772.4 in version 1.1 and 586,489,025.7 here (144 of 379 counties differ).
- County pixels are placed half a pixel off: the first longitude and latitude of each tile are read as a pixel centre, where the file gives the tile's west and north edge. This release does not measure how many pixels land in a different county or how much county mean radiance would change. The numbers are kept as they are.
- Connecticut uses the eight 2020 counties; the 2024 file has nine planning regions. The storm records, the declared lists and the customer table use the old counties.
- Hurricane Eta stays as two rows. AL292020 is the NHC storm, and DR-4588 is FEMA's North Carolina disaster declaration titled Tropical Storm Eta. Every county declared for DR-4588 is also declared for AL292020. In those counties AL292020 dates the impact from the track, one day after the FEMA incident begin date that DR-4588 uses, so their night-light and outage values for those counties differ. `storms.csv` therefore has one row more than it has distinct storms. Count Eta once when counting storms.
- Bedford city, Virginia (51515) is declared but is not in the boundary file; it is listed in `declared_unmatched`. That table holds 4 rows, all for 51515: AL062018, AL182012, DR-4072, DR-4644. Their outage rows in `utility_by_county.csv` have an empty `county`.
- `in_nhc_wind_radius` is filled for the 34 storms with a HURDAT2 34-knot wind radius on file. Empty means no radius is on file for the storm. It does not mean the county was outside the radius.
- EAGLE-I coverage is incomplete in early years and in some states, and `customers_total` is an estimate: each state's EIA-861 customer count split across counties by Census housing units. Where the peak is above the estimate the peak is published as reported, and the share is empty with a reason.
- Where the 15-minute series does not reproduce the published peak, the restore hours are empty with reason `peak_mismatch` and the peak is left as published.
- The word outage still names night-light states: the `status` value `no_measurable_outage`, the columns `outage_min_ratio` and `outage_min_day`, and the reason code `no_outage_measured`. They describe the night-light series and say nothing about reported outages.
- `valid_pixel_share` and `snow_excluded_share` have different bases (all county pixels, and pixels with a finite radiance), so the two can add to more than 1.
